claims.text: Systematically varying elemental ratios in HfNbTaTiZr will alter its mechanical properties.
Departures from the equiatomic composition will change yield strength and ductility through lattice distortion and possible phase segregation.
The initial material is equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr produced through powder metallurgy from blended powders.
The starting powders are high-purity and include both hydride and elemental powders.
Combinatorial 3D ink-extrusion printing with tailored inks can produce a continuous non-equiatomic Hf-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr composition library.
HfNbTaTiZr can be sintered at 1400 °C.
Vacuum or inert-atmosphere sintering at 1400 °C with controlled cooling will ensure uniform microstructures and comparable oxygen contamination across the composition library.
Changing composition will alter local lattice distortion, grain-size distribution, and phase fractions.
Adjusting constituent percentages changes atomic-size mismatch and solid-solution strengthening.
Hf is a relatively large atom, so increasing its fraction is expected to increase lattice distortion.
Greater lattice distortion creates stronger barriers to dislocation motion.
Departures in Nb or Ta concentration may destabilize the single-phase solid solution and promote secondary phases.
Secondary phases produced by compositional deviations can influence ductility.
Increasing Hf above its equiatomic level will increase yield strength through lattice distortion and solid-solution hardening.
Higher Hf content may reduce ductility if segregation or brittle secondary phases develop.
Compositional changes that reduce lattice distortion may lower strength and improve ductility.
The equiatomic powder-metallurgy HfNbTaTiZr alloy provides a baseline for microstructure and mechanical-property comparisons.
The proposed hypothesis is restricted to compositions retaining a single-phase or near-single-phase solid solution.
XRD and SEM can be used to assess the phases and microstructure of HfNbTaTiZr samples.
A lack of statistically significant, systematic mechanical-property changes or microstructural correlations relative to the equiatomic baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
